unit: per job: recover, evacuate and recharge the A/C system with the specified refrigerant to the maker's stated charge. No leak repair, no leak diagnosis and no parts other than refrigerant (compressor oil and dye not included)

finding: There is no live range for this job on the site today (live is null), so this is a first build, not a check. Refrigerant type decides the price: the two R-134a examples build to well under the two R-1234yf examples. Built totals (refrigerant at the maker's stated charge x a posted price per ounce, plus stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2016 Civic (R-1234yf, 13.2-15.0 oz) about $139-$392; midsize 2016 Pilot (R-1234yf, 23.8-25.6 oz) about $184-$477; truck 2016 F-150 2.7L (R-134a, 24 oz) about $59-$288; luxury 2015 Acura RDX (R-134a, 15.2-16.9 oz) about $51-$274. The low ends are not prices anyone will be quoted: they pair a retail can price ($0.97/oz R-134a, $4.19/oz R-1234yf) with a warranty time, and for R-134a that time (0.3 hr) is an add-on to a condenser job, not a stand-alone visit. The high ends use the only dealer per-ounce prices found ($2.00/oz R-134a, $8.00/oz R-1234yf) and are the more realistic guide. Posted menu prices sit at or above our high ends: R-134a from $175 to $302 and R-1234yf from $300 to $500, against benchmarks of $219-$410 that mostly do not split by refrigerant. A supportable range for the site is roughly $175-$300 for R-134a cars and $300-$500 for R-1234yf cars, with larger systems (rear A/C, more than about 1.5-2 lb) above that. How solid the labor times are: only the midsize figure is for the example vehicle (Honda's 0.7 hr warranty time for the 2016 Pilot). The Civic borrows that Honda time; the F-150 and RDX low ends borrow a GM add-on time for full-size SUVs (0.3 hr for R-134a, read by position in a table whose columns are not labelled; the same bulletin gives 1.2 hr for R-1234yf, raised from 0.5). The high ends are general: a trade-press report of the MOTOR guide's 1.7 hr for R-1234yf and one chain's '60-90 min' for the service. No Ford or Acura time was found. Refrigerant prices: there was no usable maker list price per ounce (the Honda/Acura R-1234yf part lists at $1,299.63 with no container size on the page), so the low end is a retail can price and the high end is one Ford dealer's menu rate, applied to all four classes. Charge amounts come from each vehicle's owner's manual; the F-150 figure is for the 2.7L only. Posted menu prices were found from 6 sellers (2 chains, 2 independents, 2 dealers) in 7 states; the two dealer entries price the labor only and add refrigerant on top, and no national chain prints a price for this service on the pages loaded. Reviewer note (2026-11-20): GM's 0.3 hr 'ADD: Evacuate and Recharge with R134A' is an add-on to a condenser job, so it is a cross-check and no longer a range end; the R-134a lows now use Honda's stand-alone 0.7 hr (not the example vehicles). Built totals at $120-$160/hr are now about $107-$288 for the F-150 and $99-$274 for the RDX. The built lows still pair a retail can price with a warranty time, so posted menu prices are the better guide to a real bill.
extras: A recharge on its own does not fix a leak, and a system that is low has usually leaked. A quote often adds an A/C performance check or diagnosis (posted prices seen: $59.95 to $189), leak-detection dye, compressor oil, a surcharge for recovering contaminated refrigerant (one shop: from $50), extra refrigerant beyond the amount a menu price includes (larger systems and rear A/C), a cabin air filter, shop supplies and sales tax. If a leak is found, the repair (O-rings, a hose, the condenser, the compressor) is quoted separately and the system has to be evacuated and recharged again afterwards.
